title: SEBI’s Credit Risk-o-Meter may make bond risks easier to compare - The HinduBusinessLine
text:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (SEBI) new Credit Risk-o-Meter could make it easier for retail investors to compare debt investments by translating credit ratings into six colour-coded risk categories, addressing a common difficulty in interpreting ratings assigned by different credit rating agencies.

The regulator has mandated, effective in 45 days, the meter for listed and proposed-to-be-listed non-convertible securities, commercial papers, securitised debt instruments, security receipts and structured debt or market-linked debentures, whether issued through public issues or private placements.

The framework maps existing credit ratings to six categories, ranging from lowest credit risk to high or very high risk of default.

The meter must appear in offer documents, abridged prospectuses, private placement memorandums, advertisements and the websites and mobile applications of online bond platform providers (OBPPs).

Gibin John, Senior Investment Strategist at Geojit Investments, said differences in how rating agencies present ratings for the same bond could confuse investors assessing the underlying risk. “A common Risk-o-Meter will help investors easily understand the risk level of bonds in a standardized and uniform manner,” he said, adding that the framework could improve investor confidence in debt investments by providing a clearer assessment of risk.

The standardisation is intended to help investors compare securities more easily, but the meter will not replace credit ratings. Issuers and OBPPs must also disclose the name of the rating agency and the actual rating assigned to the security.

Where a security has ratings from multiple agencies, the meter must reflect the lowest rating, although all ratings may be disclosed alongside it.

Makarand M Joshi, founding partner of corporate compliance firm MMJC & Associates, said the initiative would simplify risk communication by converting technical terminology into colour-coded indicators.

The measure could be significant for a corporate bond market valued at more than ₹45 lakh crore, where retail investors account for less than 3 per cent of holdings. A simpler way to assess and compare credit risk could encourage greater participation, he said.

However, the meter is only an indicator of credit risk. SEBI’s framework specifies that it does not constitute investment advice or a recommendation to invest. Debt securities also carry market and liquidity risks, which investors must consider separately.

For investors, the immediate benefit is a standardised visual indicator alongside existing disclosures. Whether this translates into higher retail participation will depend on investors’ understanding of debt products and their willingness to assess risks beyond the colour-coded rating.
